query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Selective thermal processing that triggers phase‐selective recrystallization of the soft fcc phase in a lamellar eutectic high‐entropy alloy will simultaneously enhance both strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a dual-phase lamellar microstructure composed of ductile fcc and hard B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment designed to induce phase-selective recrystallization that fully recrystallizes the fcc phase while preserving the interconnected B2 framework.
generation.conditions: Annealing at a temperature and duration optimized to recrystallize only the fcc phase (under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation) with subsequent cooling so that the lamellar morphology is largely maintained; tensile testing conducted at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined composite microstructure where a fully recrystallized soft (fcc) phase is embedded within a skeleton of the hard (B2) phase, resulting in coherent interfaces that promote effective strain partitioning.
generation.mechanism: By selectively recrystallizing the fcc phase, weak interphase boundaries are reduced and its strain hardening capacity is fully activated, while the continuous B2 phase provides a high-strength load-bearing network. This synergy alleviates the traditional strength-ductility trade-off.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast state, the heat-treated alloy is expected to exhibit a noticeable increase in both ultimate tensile strength and uniform elongation (for example, an increase in ductility potentially from ~10–20% to ~35% and strength improvement toward or above 2 GPa), although the exact values will depend on processing parameters.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic microstructure with unmodified lamellar distribution of fcc and B2 phases.
generation.boundary: The improvement is contingent on precise control of the heat treatment to avoid coarsening of the B2 phase or incomplete recrystallization of the fcc phase; if the selective recrystallization is not achieved, the expected property enhancements may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvement is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition and processing details. Furthermore, the long-term thermal stability of the modified microstructure under service conditions remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical as-cast eutectic HEA samples. Subject one group to the phase-selective recrystallization heat treatment while keeping a control group in the as-cast state. Characterize both groups using electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) to assess the extent of fcc recrystallization and the preservation of the B2 framework, and then perform uniaxial tensile tests to measure strength and ductility.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase fraction (via EBSD)
Work hardening rate during tensile deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the as-cast samples, or if EBSD analysis does not confirm selective recrystallization of the fcc phase with retention of the B2 network, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials.
